taxonomyNote: ADW's account uses the older genus name Bufo (Bufo fowleri); NatureServe uses Anaxyrus fowleri, noting Anaxyrus was split from Bufo by Frost et al. (2006) and that some references still use Bufo.
fieldMarks: Toad 5-9.5 cm, brown, grey or olive-green, with black-edged dark back spots that each contain three or more warts and a light mid-dorsal stripe.
Belly usually whitish and almost unspotted apart from a single dark spot on the chest.
Males tend to be darker, females lighter; enlarged parotoid glands behind the eyes release a noxious secretion.
Tadpoles are short-bodied with a long tail and upper and lower fins.
behavior: Sources disagree on timing: described as completely nocturnal in one account and mostly diurnal in another; burrows during very hot or cold spells.
Adults eat insects and small terrestrial invertebrates and avoid earthworms, unlike the American toad; tadpoles scrape algae.
Inactive in fall, winter and early spring; hybridizes with the American toad in some areas.
habitat: Wooded areas, river valleys and floodplains including farmland and residential areas, usually with deep friable soils; breeds in shallow marshes, rain pools, ponds and reservoirs with little current. Beach and dune habitat is also used.
range: NatureServe lists it in southern Ontario and across the eastern US from New England and Michigan south to Florida and west to Iowa, Kansas, Oklahoma and Texas.

lookalikes.name: American toad
lookalikes.howToTell: American has only one or two warts per dark back spot.
